title: Jamaica
summary: Jamaica is a Queens placename preserved through early town and purchase records.
address_label: Jamaica / Beaver Pond vicinity, Queens, NY (approximate)
map_geometry_source: Approximate general marker for historic Jamaica and the Beaver Pond vicinity cited by Tooker; not an exact purchase boundary or pond coordinate.
history_title: Jamaica Place Name And Deed Confirmation
history_content:
Jamaica is an Indigenous place name in Queens, preserved in written forms including Jemaica and Yemacah. An April 15, 1662 deed confirmation names Waumitumpacke and associates as participants in an agreement with Jamaica proprietors. [1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700; Records of Jamaica; William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911).]

No interpreter is named in the reviewed accounts of that confirmation.
translation_content:
Jamaica may derive from Algonquian-language words connected with beaver, an interpretation consistent with the nearby Beaver Pond landscape. The published comparison draws on Lenape/Delaware, Abenaki, Narragansett, Massachusett, and Mohegan forms, but it remains a later scholarly interpretation rather than the origin of the name. [2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911), pp. 75-76.]

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names connect land and culture. Indigenous place names tell the stories, narratives, histories, usage and ecological information of a place through time.”

— BC Geographical Names Office, Indigenous Place Names (2021), PDF page 2
land_loss_content: Jamaica preserves a place-name tied to beaver habitat, Indigenous families and communities, and early colonial land records in Queens. Recording the name carefully helps keep that Native and ecological context visible beneath the later urban neighborhood name.
whereintheworld_content: The map placement is an approximate general point for the historic Jamaica and Beaver Pond vicinity in Queens, not an exact boundary for the former town, the pond, or the 1656 purchase area.
